problem: The explanation of bridge PIV is technically wrong. It says each diode sees only Vm 'because two diodes share the reverse voltage around the loop'. In a bridge the two reverse-biased diodes do not share or divide the voltage. Each one independently blocks the full peak supply voltage Vm, because each is connected across the supply through a forward-conducting diode. A student will wrongly conclude that each diode blocks only Vm/2.
fix: PIV of each bridge diode is Vm. When D1 and D3 conduct, D2 and D4 are each reverse-biased directly across the supply (through a conducting diode), so each blocks the full Vm on its own. The bridge PIV is Vm, not because the diodes share voltage, but because each diode sits across the supply rather than across a whole centre-tapped secondary.

problem: The phrase 'the whole secondary voltage, which is 2Vm peak-to-centre' (and 'the full peak-to-centre voltage of both halves' in Q3) is confused wording. 'Peak-to-centre' is not a standard term and reads as if 2Vm were measured from a peak to the centre tap, which would be Vm.
fix: Say: 'when D1 conducts, D2 is reverse-biased by the full secondary voltage, that is 2Vm measured from one end of the secondary to the other'. In Q3: 'it blocks the peak voltage of the whole secondary, 2Vm'.

problem: 'The supply connects to opposite bridge corners, and the load connects across the other pair' is vague; 'corners' can be read as the four diode positions rather than the four bridge nodes.
fix: Say: 'The AC supply connects to two opposite nodes of the bridge (the junctions of D1-D2 and D3-D4), and the load connects across the other two opposite nodes, which become the DC positive and DC negative terminals.'
